text: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary word list, each step you change exactly one letter, and the result must be a word in the dictionary. Return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from begin to end — the number of words including both ends — or zero if none exists.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if I treat each word as a node and connect words that differ by exactly one letter, this is the shortest path in an unweighted graph. So BFS, and the level count is my answer. Is that the right model?
Exactly. All words are the same length, lowercase letters.
Does the end word have to be in the dictionary? If it's not, there's no way to land on it, so the answer would be zero.
Right — if it's not in the list, return zero.
Let me run through the example. Hit to cog, with dictionary hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog. One shortest ladder is hit, hot, dot, dog, cog — five words, so the answer is five.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. I could build the whole graph by comparing every pair of words — N squared times L, too slow for a big dictionary. This problem reminds me of shortest path on an unweighted graph, which is exactly what breadth-first search solves — but here I'll use an implicit graph: I never store edges. For the current word, I generate neighbors on the fly by trying all twenty-six letters at each position and checking the dictionary hash set. Then a plain level-order BFS: the first time I reach the end word, the level count is the shortest length.

Here's the plan. One: put the word list in a hash set, mark the begin word seen, and start step at one. Two: process the queue one layer at a time; for each word, try every letter at every position, and push each new dictionary word that isn't seen yet — if it's the end word, return step plus one. Three: after each full layer, step goes up by one. One thing worth flagging — I mutate the word in place to make neighbors, so after trying all twenty-six letters at position i, I must restore it before moving to position i plus one; otherwise I'd generate words that differ by two letters. And I mark a word seen the moment I push it, so it can't be enqueued twice. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. A hash set for the dictionary, a seen set, and a queue seeded with the begin word. Each round, I bind the layer size, then for every word and every position I save a copy, try a through z, skip anything not in the dictionary or already seen, and return step plus one on a hit. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — step plus plus lives outside the per-word loop, so it only increments once per BFS layer. That's what makes step a true distance.

Let's dry-run on hit to cog, with the same dictionary. Each layer adds one more word to the ladder: hot, then dot and lot, then dog and log. The row that matters is step four, processing dog and log: changing dog's d to c gives cog, which is the end word, so I return four plus one, five. The plus one is the subtle part: at step four the queue holds the fourth-level words, and cog is generated as a fifth-level word, so it's the fifth word in the ladder. If cog weren't in the dictionary, BFS would drain the queue without a hit and return zero.

Time is N times L squared times twenty-six, where N is the dictionary size and L the word length — each word spawns L times twenty-six candidates, and each one costs order L to hash and look up in the set. Space is N times L for the dictionary, seen set, and queue. Oh, one more thing — for a large dictionary I'd switch to bidirectional BFS — expand from both ends and meet in the middle, cutting the explored frontier from roughly b to the d, to two times b to the d over two. And if I needed the actual path, I'd store a parent pointer per word and backtrack.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You modeled it as unweighted shortest path and chose BFS. You used an implicit graph — generating neighbors by mutation instead of building edges — and restored the word between positions. And you kept step a true layer count for the plus one. Good work.
